question: Why do nurses perform a physical examination during primary health care?

options.B: To replace the need for a patient health history
options.D: To detect normal and abnormal clinical findings

explanation: Spotting what's normal versus what's unusual is a core nursing skill! The physical exam helps you systematically check the body to catch any changes early. You've got this!

question: How do subjective and objective data team up during patient assessment?

options.A: Subjective data replaces the physical exam entirely
options.B: Objective data is gathered only by asking the patient what they feel
options.C: Subjective data provides history while objective data provides measurable findings
options.D: Subjective and objective data are completely unrelated processes

explanation: Think of it this way: subjective data is what the patient tells you (like 'my head hurts'), while objective data is what you measure or see yourself (like a high temperature). Together, they give the full picture!

question: Which room setup is most important when getting ready for a physical exam?

options.B: A cold room temperature to prevent sweating
options.D: Open doors to encourage fresh airflow

explanation: Good lighting helps you see subtle skin changes clearly, and privacy helps your patient relax and feel secure with you. Always set the stage for comfort!

question: Your patient looks really nervous before you check their tummy (abdomen). What should you do first?

options.A: Scold the patient for being uncooperative
options.C: Proceed immediately without speaking to avoid wasting time
options.D: Explain the steps of the procedure and encourage relaxation

explanation: Kindness goes a long way! Explaining what you're about to do calms their nerves, which actually relaxes their belly muscles so you can get much more accurate exam results.

question: What is the single best way to stop germs from spreading during patient care?

options.A: Avoiding all physical contact with patients
options.C: Wearing sterile gowns at all times

explanation: Simple handwashing or using hand sanitiser is your superpower against infections. It washes away those sneaky microbes before they can jump to the next patient!

question: When is it necessary to pop on a pair of clean gloves during an exam?

options.A: When there is a risk of contact with bodily fluids or non-intact skin
options.B: Only when performing major surgical operations
options.C: Never, because gloves interfere with clinical touch
options.D: Throughout the entire shift without changing them

explanation: Standard precautions are there to protect both you and your patient. Wear gloves anytime you might touch blood, body fluids, secretions, or broken skin.

question: Which assessment technique uses a stethoscope to listen to sounds inside the body?
explanation: Auscultation is just the clinical word for listening! You use your stethoscope to tune into heartbeats, breathing sounds, and tummy rumbles.

question: Why do nurses auscultate (listen) before palpating (feeling) the abdomen?

options.A: To make the patient feel warmer
options.B: Because palpation takes too long to finish
options.C: To prevent the stethoscope from getting dirty
options.D: To avoid altering natural bowel sounds

explanation: If you press or rub the belly first (palpation), you wake up the intestines and create fake bowel sounds. Always listen first so you hear what's naturally going on!

question: Which of these measurements counts as an anthropometric assessment?
explanation: Anthropometric measurements are simply body dimensions and size—like height, weight, and waist circumference. Easy peasy!

question: Why are taking baseline vital signs so important at the start of care?

options.A: To determine the patient's insurance coverage
options.B: To replace the need for taking a medical history
options.C: To compare against future readings to detect sudden changes
options.D: To calculate the exact date of patient discharge

explanation: Baselines give you a starting point. Later on, you can check new numbers against this baseline to spot if your patient is suddenly getting worse or improving.

question: What is the big benefit of using a head-to-toe approach for a physical exam?

options.A: It requires the patient to change positions constantly
options.B: It allows the nurse to finish the examination in under two minutes
options.C: It eliminates the need to inspect the skin
options.D: It ensures a structured and thorough assessment without missing body parts

explanation: Going head-to-toe builds a solid routine. It makes sure you never accidentally skip checking an important body system!

question: During a head-to-toe check, you notice something unusual in the abdomen. What's your next move?

options.A: Ignore the finding until the patient goes home
options.B: Perform a more focused, in-depth regional assessment of the abdomen
options.C: Document it as normal variation without further check
options.D: Skip the rest of the exam and immediately discharge the patient

explanation: When you spot an abnormality, zoom in! Do a closer, focused check on that specific body area to gather all the clinical details you need.

question: How should a nurse properly document physical examination findings?

options.A: Use vague words like 'fine' or 'normal' to save time
options.B: Let patients write their own clinical findings in the chart
options.C: Record findings objectively using clear measurements and descriptive terms
options.D: Wait until the end of the work week to write all notes at once

explanation: Clear, factual, and measured notes help the rest of the healthcare team truly understand how the patient is doing without guessing.

question: You check a patient's blood pressure and find it dangerously high while they complain of severe chest pain. What do you do right away?

options.A: Erase the reading and take it again tomorrow
options.B: Wait until the shift handover meeting later that evening
options.C: Leave the patient room without telling anyone
options.D: Report the critical findings verbally to the physician immediately

explanation: Critical changes need fast action! Always speak up and report urgent findings right away to senior staff or the doctor so the patient gets help immediately.
